qs.q: A medical physiologist is demonstrating vagal control of intestinal secretions during a laboratory session. What is the primary neurotransmitter utilized by the parasympathetic nervous system to enhance mucus and enzyme secretion from intestinal crypts?
qs.e: Acetylcholine is the primary neurotransmitter of the parasympathetic nervous system (vagal stimulation) that enhances secretion and blood flow. Norepinephrine and epinephrine are primary neurotransmitters of the sympathetic nervous system.
qs.s: Secretions of the Small Intestine and Their Control: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following statements about the parasympathetic nervous system is correct?
o: Postganglionic neurons release acetylcholine at target organs.
Receptors on target organs are always nicotinic.
Ganglia are typically located far from target organs.
qs.e: In the parasympathetic nervous system, preganglionic neurons release acetylcholine, which acts on nicotinic receptors on postganglionic neurons. Postganglionic neurons then release acetylcholine at the target organs, where it acts on muscarinic receptors. Therefore, statement B is correct. Preganglionic neurons (A) release acetylcholine, not norepinephrine. Receptors on target organs (C) are muscarinic, not nicotinic
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Physiology Exam - June 5, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The parasympathetic nervous system (PNS) is the rest‑and‑digest arm of the autonomic nervous system, using the vagus and pelvic nerves to slow heart rate, increase digestion, and promote relaxation.

sections.p: The PNS counterbalances the sympathetic system, promoting energy conservation and recovery. It uses acetylcholine at ganglia and target organs.
Parasympathetic fibers originate in the brainstem (cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X) and sacral spinal cord (S2–S4).
Parasympathetic fibers run with cranial nerves and pelvic nerves, often sharing pathways with sympathetic fibers but diverging at target organs.
No dedicated blood supply; effects are mediated by neurotransmitters released at target organs.

Key nerves: CN III (oculomotor) for accommodation, CN VII (facial) for lacrimation, CN IX (glossopharyngeal) for pharyngeal reflexes, CN X (vagus) for heart, lungs, gut, and pelvic nerves for lower organs.
Slows heart rate, increases GI motility, stimulates salivation, dilates pupil, relaxes bladder, and promotes mucus secretion.
PNS dysfunction presents as dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, or bradycardia. Vagal nerve injury can cause syncope or gastroparesis.
Remember the mnemonic VAGAL: Vagus, Acetylcholine, Glandular secretion, Afferent, Lacrimation.

faq.q: What causes dry mouth in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Common causes include anticholinergic drugs, dehydration, HIV, and malnutrition.

faq.q: How to differentiate vagal from sympathetic overactivity?
faq.a: Vagal overactivity shows bradycardia and hypotension; sympathetic shows tachycardia and hypertension.

faq.q: Can herbal remedies affect the PNS?
faq.a: Yes, some herbs (e.g., kava) have cholinergic effects that can enhance parasympathetic activity.
